sources.topic: Deploying a Vite app to Vercel — environment variables, build settings

blocks.md: Your full-stack app authenticates users, reads and writes data through Supabase, and enforces Row Level Security. It works on your laptop. But 'works on my machine' is not a portfolio. The moment you paste a real URL into a message and someone else signs up, uses your app, and it just works — that is the moment it becomes real. This session is about crossing that line: tightening every rough edge, making the UI behave properly in every state, and pushing the whole thing to a public Vercel URL that will still be running next month.

blocks.canDo: ship a polished app to a public URL
blocks.md: **By the end of this session you will be able to:** add loading, empty, and error states everywhere in your app; render at least one chart for a data summary; pass a basic accessibility check (labels, alt text, keyboard nav, contrast); write a couple of tests; write a clean README; deploy to Vercel with `VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY` set; and share a public URL where a brand-new user can sign up and use the full app without hitting a single crash or blank screen.

**What separates a demo from a product is how it handles the edges.**

Every async operation in your app has four possible states: idle, loading, data, and error. A polished app renders something intentional for all four — a spinner, a friendly empty message, an inline error. Accessibility is not a bonus feature: labels, alt text, sufficient colour contrast, and keyboard focus management are required for real users and for automated audits. A chart turns raw data into insight — even a simple bar chart showing item counts adds genuine value. Tests (even two or three) prove you can refactor safely. A README lets anyone clone and run the project. And Vercel makes deployment a three-minute operation once your code is on GitHub — push, import, set one env var, done.

The Vercel Vite deployment guide covers connecting a GitHub repo, configuring the Vite build preset, and setting environment variables in the Vercel dashboard — everything you need to go from local to live.
blocks.label: Vercel — Deploy a Vite app (env vars, build settings)

blocks.md: **Tip — `VITE_` prefix is mandatory for browser env vars.** Vite only exposes variables to your frontend bundle if their name starts with `VITE_`. Set `VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY` (not `SUPABASE_KEY`, not `ANON_KEY`) in the Vercel Environment Variables panel under Settings → Environment Variables. Your Supabase URL needs the same treatment: `VITE_SUPABASE_URL`. After adding or changing env vars, trigger a fresh deployment — Vercel does not hot-reload env changes into existing builds.

blocks.task: Take your Phase 5 full-stack notes app (or any app from this course) and make it production-ready, then deploy it to a public Vercel URL. Your finished app must: 1. **Loading / empty / error states** — every data-fetching operation shows a loading indicator while in flight, a friendly empty message when there is no data, and a user-readable error message when something goes wrong. No blank screens, no raw error objects rendered to the DOM. 2. **A chart** — use a charting library (Recharts, Chart.js via react-chartjs-2, or Nivo) to visualise at least one piece of data from your app (e.g. note count over time, items by category, or a simple summary stat with a bar or pie chart). 3. **Accessibility pass** — every form input has an associated `
blocks.definitionOfDone: A public Vercel URL where you can open an incognito window, sign up as a brand-new user, use the full app (create, read, and interact with data), see at least one chart, and never hit a blank screen, a raw error, or a broken layout. The GitHub repo has a README and passing tests (`npm test` exits 0 locally).
hints:
**Start with polish: states and accessibility.** Go through every `useEffect` or Supabase query in your app and add a `loading` boolean and an `error` state. Render a `

Loading...

` (or a spinner) while loading, an `

...

` on error, and an empty-state message when the array is length 0. Then open your app and Tab through every interactive element — if focus skips something or a label is missing, fix it now. Run the browser's built-in accessibility checker (Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse → Accessibility) and address any red or amber issues before moving on.

**Add a chart and write your tests.** Install Recharts (`npm install recharts`) and pick one data array you already fetch — count items by a category field and pass the result as the `data` prop to a `<BarChart>`. For tests, create a `src/__tests__/` folder, install `vitest` and `@testing-library/react` if not already present, and write: (1) a test that renders your main list component with mock data and asserts the items appear, and (2) a test that fires a form submit and checks your handler was called. Run `npm test` until both pass. Then write your README: one paragraph about the app, the env vars (`VITE_SUPABASE_URL`, `VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY`), and the `npm install && npm run dev` commands.

**Deploy to Vercel.** Push everything to a GitHub repo (public or private — both work). Go to vercel.com, click Add New → Project, import the repo. Vercel auto-detects Vite; leave the build command as `vite build` and the output directory as `dist`. Before hitting Deploy, open Settings → Environment Variables and add `VITE_SUPABASE_URL` and `VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY` with the values from your Supabase project's API settings page. Click Deploy. When the build finishes, open the generated `.vercel.app` URL in an incognito window and walk through the full user journey — sign up, interact, check the chart, trigger an empty state and an error state. Copy the URL; that is your portfolio piece.

blocks.md:
You just shipped a deployed, production-quality full-stack app. It handles every UI state, passes an accessibility audit, renders real data in a chart, has a test suite, and lives at a public URL anyone can visit. That is not a tutorial project — that is a portfolio piece.

You built it across six phases: HTML and CSS fundamentals, React components and state, TypeScript, async data fetching, Supabase authentication and RLS, and now deployment. The next stop is the Phase 6 quiz to lock in everything you learned about shipping.
bullets: Loading / empty / error states are what separate a demo from a product — every async op needs all three
Accessibility is not optional: labels, alt text, keyboard nav, and contrast keep real users from being locked out

A README and a passing test run are the minimum bar for a project worth sharing
